p: The Seleucid king who had escaped from Rome to take his uncle's throne in 162 BC.
b: Demetrius I, called Soter ("Savior"), was the son of Seleucus IV. He spent his youth as a hostage in Rome, escaped in 162 BC, and seized the throne from the boy-king Antiochus V (7:1–4). He sent Bacchides and Alcimus once before (7:8–20), then Nicanor, who was killed on 13 Adar (7:43–49). How soon this second expedition followed depends on the year of Nicanor's defeat, which the book does not give: if it was Adar 160 BC, Judas had only weeks; many date it to 161 BC, which leaves about a year. Demetrius ruled until Alexander Balas killed him in battle in 150 BC (10:50).

p: The general who kept Judea for the king, and the high priest the king had installed.
b: Bacchides was one of the king's Friends and ruled the province Beyond the River (7:8). Alcimus (Hebrew Yakim or Eliakim) was a priest whom Demetrius confirmed as high priest (7:9; 2 Maccabees 14:3–13). Some of the pious accepted him because he was a priest descended from Aaron (7:14), and he then had sixty of them killed (7:16). For the writer he is the model of the high priest who serves a foreign king against his people; his death in 9:54–56 clears the way for Jonathan's priesthood in chapter 10.

a: the right wing of his army
p: The right wing of a Hellenistic army held its best troops, and the commander fought there.
b: In Greek and Macedonian battle order the right wing was the place of honor, where the best cavalry and the general stood (as Bacchides does in 9:12, 14). Sending "the right wing" means sending the core of the royal army, not local garrisons. This explains why Judas's men lost heart (9:6).

a: They took the road to Gilgal
p: The Greek says Galgala, but the route makes many scholars think the writer meant Galilee.
b: The Greek reads Γάλγαλα, the Greek form of Gilgal. But Gilgal by Jericho (Joshua 4:19) is far off the route, and Josephus, who retold this book, says Bacchides camped at "Arbela, a city of Galilee" (Antiquities 12.421). Arbela stands above the west shore of the Sea of Galilee, with caves where rebels later hid. So many scholars think the Hebrew original read "Galilee" (Galil) and a copyist or translator turned it into the better-known Gilgal. No manuscript has "Galilee", so the Plain keeps Gilgal.

p: Probably not a town but "the steps": the cliff paths to the caves at Arbela.
b: No town Mesaloth is known. Many scholars take the word as Hebrew mesillot, "paths, ascents", and connect it with the cliff caves of Arbela, where Herod later fought rebels hiding in the rock face (Josephus, Antiquities 14.415–430). If so, Bacchides cleared the caves where Jewish fighters or refugees had taken shelter, before marching south.

p: The year 152 of the Seleucid kings; its first month is about April 160 BC.
b: 1 Maccabees dates by the Seleucid era, counted from Seleucus I's return to Babylon in 312/311 BC. Scholars agree that the book does not always start the year at the same point: for many events in Judea it seems to count from the spring of 311 BC (from Nisan, the first month), and for royal events from the autumn of 312 BC (the Macedonian reckoning). On the spring count, the first month of 152 is Nisan (March–April) 160 BC, the usual date for Judas's death. How long that was after Nicanor's defeat in Adar depends on whether he fell in 161 or 160 BC.

p: Two villages north of Jerusalem, near Ramallah; the sites are likely but not certain.
b: Berea is usually placed at el-Bireh near Ramallah, or at Beeroth (Joshua 9:17). Elasa (9:5) is often identified with Khirbet Il'asa near Beth-horon. The battle was thus fought in the hills north of Jerusalem, near where Judas had beaten Seron (3:16–24) and Nicanor (7:39–43). Alexandrinus spells it Alasa; Sinaiticus and Venetus Elasa (KJV Eleasa).

a: until no more than eight hundred men were left
p: Like Gideon's army, Judas's force shrinks; but this time there is no promised victory.
b: Israel's story knows armies that God reduced: Gideon sent home the fearful and kept three hundred (Judges 7:2–8), and Deuteronomy tells the fearful to go home (Deuteronomy 20:8). Judas had used that law himself (3:56). Here the fearful leave on their own, and 3,000 become 800 against 22,000. The writer, who never says that God promised Judas anything, lets the reader feel how different this is from Gideon's night.

p: Judas speaks without any assurance: the Greek "if perhaps" leaves the outcome open.
b: The Greek ἐὰν ἄρα, "if perhaps", is the language of hope, not of a promise. Earlier Judas told his men that victory does not depend on numbers, because strength comes from Heaven (3:18–19). Here he says nothing about Heaven at all. The book's restraint is deliberate: it never claims that God spoke to Judas.

a: Later we will come back with our brothers and fight them
p: Judas's men proposed a fighting retreat; ancient and modern readers have weighed both choices.
b: The men's plan was sensible guerrilla warfare: save the army and fight another day, as the brothers later did (9:33–49). Judas refuses for the sake of his "glory" (9:10). The writer admires him, but also lets Jonathan survive by retreat. Some modern historians judge that Judas misjudged the odds; others note that his earlier victories had been won against similar numbers. 2 Maccabees, which ends with the defeat of Nicanor, does not tell of Judas's death at all.

a: with courage for our brothers' sake
p: Judas chooses death over flight: the Greek ideal of a noble death meets Israel's holy war.
b: "Let us die with courage (ἀνδρίᾳ) for our brothers' sake, and leave nothing to stain our glory" joins two traditions. Greek historians praised the soldier who would not flee, above all Leonidas at Thermopylae. Israel's stories praise leaders who risked their lives for the people (Judges 9:17; 1 Samuel 19:5). 1 Maccabees never speaks of a reward after death; Judas's "glory" is his name in Israel's memory (compare 6:44, where Eleazar dies to win a lasting name). Whether Christians may fight in war at all is carded at Deuteronomy 20.
orig: ἀποθάνωμεν ἀνδρίᾳ χάριν τῶν ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν

p: The Macedonian block of pikemen, the heavy center of a Seleucid army.
b: The phalanx (φάλαγξ) was the Macedonian infantry formation: men in deep ranks with pikes up to six meters long. With cavalry on the wings and light troops (slingers and archers, 9:11) in front, it was the standard Seleucid order of battle. Here the phalanx closes in "from both sides": the wings, not the center, decide the day.

a: Judas's men blew their trumpets too
p: Israel's priests blew trumpets in battle, as the law commanded.
b: Numbers 10:9 tells Israel to sound the trumpets when they go to war, with the promise, "Then the LORD your God will remember you, and you will be rescued from your enemies". Judas's army does so throughout the book (3:54; 4:13; 5:33). The Qumran War Scroll later describes priests blowing trumpets inscribed with battle slogans. Here both sides blow trumpets, and for once the sound brings no rescue.

p: Azotus is Ashdod on the coast, far from the battle; the name is probably a slip in the text.
b: Azotus is the Greek name of Ashdod, more than 40 km (25 miles) to the west on the coastal plain, and no hill near Elasa is called by that name. Scholars suggest that the Hebrew had another hill name. One proposal is "the slopes" (Hebrew ashdot, read as Ashdod). Another is Baal-hazor (2 Samuel 13:23), the highest hill north of Jerusalem, which a translator could misread. Josephus, retelling the battle, names the hill Aza (Antiquities 12.429). The pursuit, at least, carried Judas north and away from his own lines.

p: Judas Maccabeus died at Elasa in the spring of 160 BC, six years after the revolt began.
b: The book tells the death in seven Greek words: Judas fell, and the rest fled. Judas had led the revolt since his father's death in 166 BC (2:66; 3:1), retaken and cleansed the Temple (4:36–59), and defeated Nicanor (7:43–50). Josephus retells the battle from this book (Antiquities 12.420–434). His death came only months after the treaty with Rome (chapter 8), which Rome did nothing to enforce.

a: buried him in his ancestors' tomb at Modein
p: Judas is buried with Mattathias; later Simon built a great monument there.
b: Modein, the family's home town west of Jerusalem near Lod, was where the revolt began (2:1, 15–28) and where Mattathias was buried (2:70). Simon later built a tall monument with seven pyramids over the tomb, decorated with carved ships that could be seen from the sea (13:25–30). The exact site is still debated.

a: beat their breasts for him in a great lament
p: The Greek word means beating the breast: public, loud mourning.
b: The verb κόπτομαι and the noun κοπετός mean beating the breast or striking oneself in grief, the regular words in the Greek Old Testament for formal mourning (Genesis 50:10; 1 Samuel 25:1; Zechariah 12:10). "All Israel" mourning "many days" puts Judas beside Jacob (Genesis 50:10), Samuel (1 Samuel 25:1) and Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:24–25).
orig: ἐκόψαντο αὐτὸν πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ κοπετὸν μέγαν

t: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan
p: The lament borrows the refrain of David's song over Saul and Jonathan.
b: "How the warrior has fallen" takes up the refrain of David's lament: "How the warriors have fallen!" (2 Samuel 1:19). The Greek of 2 Samuel 1:19 has the same verb and the same word for "mighty" (πῶς ἔπεσαν δυνατοί). The writer sets Judas beside Saul and Jonathan, killed by Israel's enemies on the hills; and the man who buries him and takes his place is also named Jonathan. David's song is long; this lament is one line. Many scholars think the writer quoted only its opening, as a sign of a longer lament known to his readers.

p: The word "save" casts Judas as one of the judges whom God raised up to rescue Israel.
b: The Greek σῴζων, "saving", is the verb of the book of Judges, where God raised up "a rescuer" for Israel (Judges 3:9; 3:15; compare Judges 2:16). The book presents the Maccabee brothers as a new set of judges: of Jonathan it says that he "began to judge the people" (9:73). 1 Maccabees also says plainly that salvation came "by the hand" of this family (5:62).

p: The closing words copy the regnal formula of Kings, but say the record was never written.
b: The books of Kings close each reign with a formula such as "The rest of Solomon's story, all he did and his wisdom, is written in the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds, is it not?" (1 Kings 11:41). 1 Maccabees uses the same frame for Judas, but turns it: his deeds were too many to be written. The same frame closes the book for John Hyrcanus (16:23–24), and a similar turn ends the Gospel of John (John 21:25). It treats Judas as a ruler whose reign deserves the royal formula, though he was never king.

p: Two vivid verbs: the lawless peer out of hiding, then spring up like plants.
b: ἐξέκυψαν means to peep out, like an animal from its hole. ἀνέτειλαν is used of the sun rising or plants sprouting. Together they say that the renegades had been in hiding while Judas lived and came out as soon as he died. The lawless (ἄνομοι) are Jews who favored the Greek way of life and the king's high priest, not foreigners (compare 1:11; 7:5).

p: Hunger, not only fear, drove the countryside to the king's side.
b: The war had stripped the farms of Judea. 1 Maccabees mentions a Sabbatical year that emptied the stores two years before (6:49, 53), and armies lived off the land. When Judas died, the hungry villages went over to the side that could feed them and stop the fighting. The Greek αὐτομολέω is the word for soldiers deserting to the enemy.

p: The book's word for the Jews who sided with the Seleucids against the Torah party.
b: 1 Maccabees divides Israel into the loyal and the "ungodly" (ἀσεβεῖς), "lawless" (ἄνομοι) and "renegades" (παράνομοι). Historians see in these labels the Hellenizing party, who wanted Judea to live as a Greek city under the king (1:11–15), and also traditional priests who accepted Alcimus. Their own account of the war has not survived.

a: since the day a prophet was last seen among them
p: 1 Maccabees knows that no prophet has spoken for a long time, and waits for one.
b: The writer dates Israel's worst distress by the end of prophecy. Twice more the book says that no prophet is present: the stones of the defiled altar are stored "until a prophet should come" (4:46), and Simon is made leader "until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41). Psalm 74:9 already laments, "There is no prophet now." Josephus says that the exact line of prophets ended with Artaxerxes (Against Apion 1.41), and the rabbis taught that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died "the holy spirit departed from Israel" (Tosefta Sotah 13:3; Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 9b). Whether this statement tells against the book's own place in the canon is the question of a card on the book's opening page; whether prophecy continues in the church is carded at Numbers 11.
orig: ἀφ᾽ ἧς ἡμέρας οὐκ ὤφθη προφήτης αὐτοῖς

p: The phrase echoes Daniel's "time of distress such as there has not been", written in the same war.
b: "Great distress (θλῖψις) ... such as had not been" is close to Daniel 12:1, "a time of distress such as there has not been since there was a nation", which most scholars date to the same war, about 165 BC. Jesus uses the same language for the coming distress in Jerusalem (Matthew 24:21; Mark 13:19). 1 Maccabees measures its distress by history, not by the end of the world: it was the worst since prophecy stopped.

p: Judas's men choose his youngest surviving brother, called Apphus, to lead them.
b: Jonathan, surnamed Apphus (2:5), was the youngest of Mattathias's five sons. He is chosen by the loyalists themselves, not by any king or priest: "ruler and leader" (ἄρχων, ἡγούμενος) are military titles here. For eight years he led a small band in the wilderness; only in 152 BC did a king make him high priest (10:20). Josephus says that Judas was high priest, but 1 Maccabees never says so, and most historians follow 1 Maccabees.

p: The dry hills south of Bethlehem, where David hid from Saul and Amos kept flocks.
b: Tekoa lies about 8 km (5 miles) south of Bethlehem, on the edge of the Judean desert that falls away to the Dead Sea. It was Amos's home (Amos 1:1) and the region where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23–24). The cistern of Asphar is unknown (for the spelling, see the variant). Like David, Jonathan begins his career as a fugitive in the desert.

a: Bacchides learned of it on the Sabbath day
p: This verse seems to anticipate 9:43, and many scholars think it is a copy of it.
b: Verse 34 says that Bacchides came across the Jordan on the Sabbath, but the story goes on to John's convoy (9:35–42) and only then tells of Bacchides coming to the Jordan on the Sabbath (9:43). Many commentators think verse 34 is an early scribe's copy of verse 43, put in the wrong place. Others read it as a summary heading for the whole episode. The Sabbath detail matters: since Mattathias's decision (2:41), the Jews fought back on the Sabbath when attacked.

p: The brother is John, the eldest son of Mattathias; the Greek names him only in the next verse.
b: John, called Gaddi (2:2), is the only brother of whom the book tells almost nothing until his death. "At the head of the crowd" (ἡγούμενον τοῦ ὄχλου) probably means he led the convoy of families and goods, not the fighters. The KJV adds the name John here; the Greek has it in 9:36. 2 Maccabees 8:22 lists a "Joseph" among Judas's brothers instead of John, probably by mistake.

p: The Arab traders of Petra, who had already shown friendship to Judas.
b: The Nabataeans were an Arab people whose capital was Petra in what is now Jordan. They grew rich on the incense trade. They had met Judas peacefully and told him about the Jews of Gilead (5:25). Here Jonathan hopes to leave his baggage with them east of the Jordan. Later, Aretas, a Nabataean king, governed Damascus in Paul's day (2 Corinthians 11:32).

a: the sons of Jambri came out of Medeba
t: Medeba and the sons of Jambri
p: An Arab clan of Medeba, east of the Dead Sea.
b: Medeba (modern Madaba in Jordan) is an old Moabite town named in Numbers 21:30 and Isaiah 15:2. The "sons of Jambri" were a clan there, known only from this story; Josephus, retelling it, calls them "the sons of Amaraeus" (Antiquities 13.11). John Hyrcanus later captured Medeba after a long siege (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255).

a: one of the great nobles of Canaan
p: A biblical name for the old non-Israelite peoples of the land, here a contemptuous label for the bride's family.
b: "Canaan" had long ceased to be a real people's name. By calling the bride's father a noble "of Canaan", the writer casts the clan as the old enemies whom Joshua fought. The place Nadabath is unknown; Sinaiticus has Gabadan and Venetus Nabadath.

a: The wedding became a time of mourning
p: The words echo the prophets' threat that God would turn Israel's songs into laments.
b: Amos warns, in God's name, "I will turn your feasts into mourning" (Amos 8:10), and Jeremiah that the sound of the bridegroom and bride will cease (Jeremiah 7:34). 1 Maccabees turns the prophets' words against Israel's enemies: this time it is the foreign wedding that becomes a funeral. The same reversal appears in 1:39–40, where Jerusalem's feasts were turned into mourning.

p: The Jordan's banks are a strip of reed marsh and thicket, where Jonathan's men could hide.
b: The Jordan runs through a narrow belt of reed beds, tamarisk and willow below the dry terraces of the valley. Jeremiah calls it, literally, "the pride of the Jordan" (Hebrew ge'on ha-yarden), a thicket where lions lived (Jeremiah 12:5; Jeremiah 49:19). Jonathan's men hide there, and 9:45 describes the same ground: water on both sides, "marsh and thicket". For the manuscripts' "mountain", see the variant.

a: Today is not like the days before
p: A Hebrew idiom for "as before": this time there is no way out.
b: The Greek "not as yesterday and the third day" copies a Hebrew idiom (kitmol shilshom), "as formerly", seen in Genesis 31:2 and 1 Samuel 19:7. It is one of many signs that 1 Maccabees was written in Hebrew and translated word for word.

p: 1 Maccabees never uses the word "God" in its narrative; it says "Heaven".
b: The Greek εἰς οὐρανόν, "to heaven", stands for God, as in Daniel 4:26 ("Heaven rules") and Jesus' "kingdom of heaven" in Matthew. In its best texts 1 Maccabees avoids the words "God" and "Lord" in the story, and uses "Heaven" in prayers and speeches (3:18–19, 50, 60; 4:10, 24, 55). Scholars explain it as reverence, a habit of later Jewish speech; it does not mean the book is less religious. The Plain writes Heaven with a capital.

a: swam across to the other side
p: Jonathan escapes east across the river, where the Seleucid cavalry would not follow.
b: The Jordan near Jericho is narrow but fast, and in spring it floods (Joshua 3:15). Jonathan's men swam to the east bank. The text does not say how a thousand of Bacchides' men fell, but a fight at the riverbank against a force that can retreat into marsh is costly. Bacchides then turned to holding Judea with forts (9:50–52).

p: The forts guarded the roads into the Judean hills from every side.
b: The list names fortresses at the edges of Judea: Jericho in the east; Emmaus and Beth-horon on the western roads up from the coast; Bethel to the north; Timnath and Pharathon in the northwestern hills (the Greek may name one place, Timnath-pharathon); Tephon, perhaps Tappuah. With Beth-zur in the south, Gazara (Gezer) on the coast road, and the Citadel in Jerusalem (9:52), they let the government control the roads without holding every village. Archaeologists have found Hellenistic fort walls at some of these sites, such as Beth-zur, but which walls belong to Bacchides is debated.

p: A border fortress on the road south toward Hebron, held by each side in turn.
b: Beth-zur (Khirbet et-Tubeiqa), about 30 km (19 miles) south of Jerusalem, guarded the road from Idumea. Judas fortified it after cleansing the Temple (4:61; 6:7), it surrendered to Antiochus V's army in 6:49–50, and Bacchides now strengthens it again. It becomes the last refuge of the renegades (10:14) until Simon takes it (11:65–66). Whether "the city" in this verse is Beth-zur itself or Jerusalem is set out in the variant.

p: Hostages from leading families kept the country quiet; Jonathan freed them in 10:9.
b: Taking the sons of leading men was the normal way for Hellenistic kings to hold a province: Demetrius himself had grown up as a hostage in Rome (7:1). The boys in the Citadel tied their families to the king. Demetrius later handed them to Jonathan to win him over (10:6, 9).

a: the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary
p: Alcimus began to remove a wall in the Temple courts; scholars debate which one.
b: Two explanations are common. Some think the wall divided the court of Israel from an outer court where Gentiles could come, so that Alcimus opened the holy area to foreigners; Josephus later describes the stone barrier that warned Gentiles not to go farther (Jewish War 5.193–194). Others think of the wall around the inner court that the returned exiles had built. Either way, the writer counts it as an attack on the holiness of the sanctuary. The Latin has "the walls of the inner holy house".
orig: τὸ τεῖχος τῆς αὐλῆς τῶν ἁγίων τῆς ἐσωτέρας

p: The Temple rebuilt under Haggai and Zechariah, whom Ezra calls the prophets of the rebuilding.
b: The second Temple was built in 520–515 BC, when, in Ezra's words, "the prophets, Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo" spoke to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem (Ezra 5:1), and the elders built "as Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied" (Ezra 6:14). The writer sees Alcimus tearing down what prophets had built, and so attacking God's own work. The phrase links back to 9:27: prophets no longer arise, but their work still stands, and touching it brings judgment.

p: Like other enemies of the Temple, Alcimus dies by a sudden stroke.
b: ἐπλήγη, "was struck", is the language of a blow from God, though the book does not name God. He loses speech and is paralyzed, perhaps by a stroke. The pattern is common in Jewish and Christian writing: Antiochus IV dies of a painful disease (6:8–16; 2 Maccabees 9:5–28), Heliodorus is flogged by angels (2 Maccabees 3:24–28), and Herod Agrippa is "struck" by an angel (Acts 12:23). Josephus says Alcimus died after four years as high priest, but he puts the death before Judas's, and has the people then make Judas high priest (Antiquities 12.413–414).

a: Alcimus died at that time in great agony
t: Seven years without a high priest
p: After Alcimus died in 159 BC, no high priest is named until Jonathan in 152 BC.
b: 1 Maccabees names no high priest between Alcimus's death (9:56) and Jonathan's appointment (10:20). Josephus gives two figures: in one place the city was without a high priest for seven years (Antiquities 20.237); in another Jonathan put on the robe four years after Judas's death (Antiquities 13.46). Elsewhere again he makes Judas high priest (Antiquities 12.414, 434). Some scholars think the office was not empty: they suggest a high priest whose name was left out because he was not a Hasmonean, perhaps the Teacher of Righteousness of the Dead Sea Scrolls (see the chapter 10 page).

a: the land of Judah was quiet for two years
p: The words echo the refrain of Judges: "the land was quiet" for so many years.
b: ἡσύχασεν ἡ γῆ, "the land was quiet", is the refrain of Judges after each rescue: "So the land was quiet for forty years" (Judges 3:11; compare Judges 3:30; Judges 5:31; Judges 8:28). The same words return in 11:38 and 11:52 for Demetrius II, and in 14:4 for Simon. The two quiet years were 159–157 BC.
orig: καὶ ἡσύχασεν ἡ γῆ Ἰούδα ἔτη δύο

a: and he put them to death
p: The Greek shifts from "they seized" to "he killed"; Josephus makes the killer Bacchides, turning on his own allies.
b: "They seized" (συνέλαβον) and "he killed" (ἀπέκτεινεν) have no named subject. Josephus makes Bacchides the killer: angry with the renegades who had misled him and the king, he put fifty of their leaders to death (Antiquities 13.25), as his army turns on them again in 9:69. Some readers take "they seized" as Jonathan's men, striking first at the plotters of 9:58–60. Sinaiticus lacks the number fifty.

p: A ruined fort in the desert near Tekoa, probably Khirbet Beit Bassa.
b: Bethbasi is usually placed at Khirbet Beit Bassa, about 3 km (2 miles) east of Bethlehem, on the edge of the wilderness of Tekoa (9:33). Jonathan rebuilt its "torn-down parts": it was an old ruin. The siege that follows (9:64–68) is the first time the brothers hold a fortified place of their own against a royal army.

a: Odomera and his brothers and the sons of Phasiron
p: Bedouin chiefs of the desert who had taken the king's side or blocked Jonathan.
b: Odomera and the sons of Phasiron are not known elsewhere. They lived "in their tents", so they were nomads of the Judean desert. Jonathan's raid on them removed Bacchides' local allies and fed his own men while Simon held the fort.

p: "They" are most likely Bacchides' army, turning on the renegades who had promised an easy win.
b: The Greek "they were angry ... and they killed many of them" follows straight after "they pressed him hard", where "they" are Simon's men. But the sentence goes on "and he decided to go back to his land", which is Bacchides. Most readers, with the KJV and the Latin (which read "he"), take the anger as Bacchides' own. See the variant.
orig: καὶ ὠργίσθησαν θυμῷ τοῖς ἀνδράσιν τοῖς ἀνόμοις

p: A truce, not a treaty with the king: Bacchides gives his own oath.
b: Jonathan's envoys made peace with Bacchides, the general, who swore not to harm him and gave back prisoners. Nothing is said of the king. The truce left Jonathan the most powerful man in the Judean countryside, with the Citadel and the forts still in Seleucid hands, until the civil war of 152 BC made both kings court him.

p: Another Jonathan made Michmash famous: Saul's son, who beat the Philistines there.
b: Michmash (Greek Machmas) lies about 11 km (7 miles) north of Jerusalem, across a gorge from Geba. There Jonathan son of Saul and his armor bearer climbed the cliff and routed the Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 13:23; 1 Samuel 14:1–14). The writer, who has just echoed David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (9:21), lets the new Jonathan settle at the place of the old one's victory. Michmash was resettled after the exile (Nehemiah 11:31).

a: He began to judge the people
p: The verb "judge" makes Jonathan a ruler like Israel's judges, before any king gave him a title.
b: κρίνειν, "to judge", is the word for the rule of Israel's judges (Judges 3:10; Judges 10:2) and of Samuel (1 Samuel 7:15). Jonathan rules the people without office or title, from a village base, as Samuel ruled from his circuit. "The sword came to rest" recalls the refrain of Judges, "the land was quiet" (Judges 3:11). Many historians see these years (157–152 BC) as the time when the Hasmoneans quietly became the real government of the Judean countryside.

p: A young man who claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV; most ancient writers called him an impostor.
b: Alexander, called Balas in later writers, claimed to be the son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Polybius, who knew the court politics of the time, says he was put forward with Laodice, a daughter of Antiochus, by Heraclides, an enemy of Demetrius, and that the Roman Senate gave him leave to seek the throne (Polybius 33.18). Other ancient writers say he was of humble birth. He had the support of Attalus II of Pergamum and Ptolemy VI of Egypt. 1 Maccabees never questions his claim; it calls him "the son of Antiochus".

p: The port of Acco, the chief royal city on the coast north of Mount Carmel.
b: Ptolemais is Acco (Judges 1:31), renamed by the Ptolemies of Egypt. The "year 160" is 152 BC. The city's garrison welcomed Alexander, perhaps because Demetrius was unpopular with his army. It becomes the stage of this chapter: the royal wedding (10:57–58), Jonathan's investiture in purple (10:60–65) and, later, Jonathan's capture by Tryphon (12:45–48).

p: Two rival kings now compete for Jonathan's support, and he gains from both.
b: From 152 BC the Seleucid kingdom was split between rival kings, and each needed the small but tough Jewish army. Demetrius offers first: the right to raise troops and the release of the hostages (10:6). Alexander answers with the high priesthood (10:20). Demetrius replies with a huge list of gifts (10:25–45). Historians see here the method by which the Hasmoneans won independence: not by one great victory, but by selling their loyalty to the highest bidder in the Seleucid civil wars.

p: σύμμαχος: a fighting partner. A Seleucid king now treats Jonathan's band as an allied army.
b: The word σύμμαχος means "one who fights alongside". In 9:60 it was the word for the Jewish renegades who sided with Bacchides. Now the king offers it to Jonathan. The change of words tells the reversal: the rebel band has become a power the king must bargain with.

a: Jonathan made his home in Jerusalem
p: After eight years in the countryside, Jonathan moves into Jerusalem, with the Citadel still held against him.
b: Jonathan had ruled from Michmash (9:73). The letter gave him the right to raise troops, and the Citadel's garrison could no longer stop him. He rebuilt the walls of the Temple mount, which had been torn down under Antiochus V (6:62). The Citadel itself held out until Simon took it in 141 BC (13:49–52).

p: In 1 Maccabees, Mount Zion is the Temple mount, not the city of David.
b: In the books of Samuel, Zion is David's fortress (2 Samuel 5:7). In 1 Maccabees "Mount Zion" is the hill of the Temple, set over against the Citadel, which stood in the "city of David" (1:33; 4:37, 60; 7:33). Jonathan fortifies the sacred hill, the Temple mount, so that the Citadel cannot again reach the sanctuary.

a: those who had abandoned the law and the commandments
p: Jewish renegades held out at Beth-zur until Simon took it in 11:65–66.
b: The foreign troops in Bacchides' forts went home (10:12–13), but the Jews who had sided with the king could not: their own people would not receive them. Beth-zur, on the border with Idumea, became their refuge. Simon finally took it, let the defenders go and put his own garrison there (11:65–66).

a: King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings
p: Kings called client rulers "brother": a title of courtesy, not a claim of equality.
b: Hellenistic kings addressed favored vassals and allied rulers as "brother" (ἀδελφός), as did the kings of the ancient Near East (1 Kings 9:13; 1 Kings 20:32). Demetrius II uses the same address (11:30). The greeting χαίρειν, "rejoice", is the usual opening of a Greek letter, as in Acts 15:23 and James 1:1.

a: So today we appoint you high priest of your nation
t: A high priest made by a pagan king
p: Jonathan's high priesthood comes from a Seleucid king's letter, not from Aaron's line by right of birth.
b: By the Torah, the high priest came from Aaron's line, and from Solomon's time the family of Zadok held the office (1 Kings 2:35; 1 Chronicles 6:3–15). The last high priest of that family in Jerusalem, Onias III, had been deposed and killed (2 Maccabees 4:7–34); his son Onias IV fled to Egypt and, under Ptolemy VI, built a temple at Leontopolis (Josephus, Antiquities 13.62–73). Since then the kings had sold or given the office (Jason, Menelaus, Alcimus). Jonathan was of a priestly family, the course of Joarib (2:1; 1 Chronicles 24:7), but not of the high priestly house. Here the office comes from Alexander's letter, and 1 Maccabees tells it without apology. See the chapter page.

p: A rank at the Seleucid court. "Friends" were the king's council and officers.
b: The Seleucid court had graded ranks: Friends (φίλοι), First Friends (πρῶτοι φίλοι, 10:65; 11:27) and Kinsmen (συγγενεῖς, 10:89; 11:31). The titles brought robes, privileges and duties. Mattathias had refused to become a Friend of the King by sacrificing (2:18). His son accepts the title as a reward from a king who demands no sacrifice.

a: a purple robe and a gold crown
p: The marks of royal favor: purple was the color of kings and their high officials.
b: Purple dye, made from murex shells, was costly, and by law or custom only the king and those he honored could wear it. A gold crown or wreath was the gift of a king to a favored subject. The book's readers knew that Jonathan's successors wore these marks by right: Simon is honored with purple and gold in 14:43–44, and the Hasmoneans after him became kings.

t: Jonathan's first service as high priest
p: Jonathan put on the high priest's vestments at the Feast of Booths in October 152 BC.
b: "The holy robe" (ἡ ἁγία στολή) is the high priest's dress, the "holy clothes" made "for glory and for beauty" (Exodus 28:2). The Feast of Booths in the seventh month of 160 fell in the autumn of 152 BC. It was the great pilgrim feast, with crowds in Jerusalem, and the high priest's role at it was public. The writer gives the exact date, as for the Temple's dedication (4:52), because a new line of high priests began that day.

a: He gathered troops and made many weapons
p: The same verse puts Jonathan in priestly robes and at the head of an army.
b: Jonathan's first act after the vestments is to raise troops and weapons. For the book's first readers, under high priests who were also generals and, from 104 BC, kings, this union of altar and sword was normal. For their critics, such as the authors of some Dead Sea Scrolls and later the Pharisees who asked a Hasmonean to give up the priesthood (Josephus, Antiquities 13.288–292), it was the problem.

a: King Demetrius to the nation of the Jews, greetings
t: A letter to the nation, not to Jonathan
p: Demetrius writes to "the nation of the Jews", passing over Jonathan, whom Alexander had just honored.
b: Alexander's letter was to "his brother Jonathan" (10:18); Demetrius's long letter is addressed to the nation. Many historians see this as a sign that the letter is a real document: Demetrius would not recognize the high priest his rival had made, and tried to win the people over his head. Josephus, retelling the letter, addresses it to "Jonathan and the nation" (Antiquities 13.48), perhaps to tidy the difference.

p: The letter lists the taxes the Seleucids collected: tribute, salt tax, crown money and shares of the harvest.
b: The letter gives a rare inside view of Seleucid taxation. Tribute (φόροι) was the province's payment; the salt tax came from the Dead Sea salt; "crowns" (στέφανοι) were gold crowns once offered freely to a king and later collected as a tax; and the king took a third of the grain and half of the tree fruit (10:30). These rates are very high, which is one reason some historians think the letter exaggerates. Antiochus III's decree for Jerusalem, in Josephus, already freed the council, priests and Temple staff from the crown tax and other taxes (Antiquities 12.142–144).
orig: τῆς τιμῆς τοῦ ἁλός, καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν στεφάνων

a: the three districts added to it from Samaria and Galilee
p: Aphairema, Lydda and Rathamin, named in 11:34: border districts south of Samaria.
b: The districts (νομοί) are named in 11:34: Aphairema (Ophrah or Ephraim, northeast of Bethel), Lydda (Lod) and Rathamin (Ramathaim, Samuel's town). They lay between Judea and Samaria and had a largely Jewish population. "And Galilee" here is odd, since none of the three is in Galilee; many think it is a slip. This verse only promises; 11:34 confirms the grant.

a: its tithes and tolls as well
p: The Greek is a bare list; it may mean the city keeps its tithes and tolls, or is freed from them.
b: The Greek says only "let Jerusalem be holy and free, and its territory, the tithes and the tolls". It may mean that Jerusalem's territory is free of royal tithes and tolls (so the KJV, "free ... from tenths and tributes"), or that the tithes and tolls go to Jerusalem itself (so the Latin and Douay, "let the tenths and tributes be for itself"). The Plain leaves it open. The "tithe" here is a royal tax, not the priestly tithe of Numbers 18:21.

a: All the feasts and Sabbaths and new moons and appointed days
p: The king promises that no tax or legal claim will be pressed on Jews on their holy days.
b: "Exemption and release" (ἀτέλεια, ἄφεσις) meant that Jews would not be summoned to court or made to pay on their holy days, and for three days before and after each festival, so pilgrims could travel. Later Roman decrees for Jews of the Diaspora gave similar protection: freedom from army service, since they could not march on the Sabbath (Josephus, Antiquities 14.226–227), and no summons to court on the Sabbath (16.163). The promise answers the persecution of 1:45, when the king forbade Sabbaths and feasts.

p: Jews served as soldiers in Hellenistic armies; the promise is that they may keep their own laws there.
b: Jewish troops had long served foreign kings: the Persian garrison at Elephantine in Egypt, and Jewish soldiers under the Ptolemies. The offer to enroll 30,000 is large but in keeping with royal habits. The key promise is in 10:37: Jewish officers, and the right "to live by their own laws", which would include the Sabbath and food laws. Jewish troops do serve Demetrius II at Antioch in 11:44–51.

a: Ptolemais and the land belonging to it
t: A gift that was not his
p: Demetrius gives away Ptolemais, which Alexander held: a sign of desperation, or of invention?
b: Alexander had seized Ptolemais (10:1), so Demetrius gives the Temple a city he did not control. Some historians count this, with the very high tax rates, as a reason to doubt that the letter is genuine as it stands. Others think it is exactly what a desperate king would promise: it costs him nothing now and makes the Jews his allies against Alexander. The Hasmoneans did not gain Ptolemais until much later, and then only briefly.

a: Whoever flees to the Temple in Jerusalem
p: The Temple is made a place of refuge for debtors to the king, as many Greek temples were.
b: Greek temples, such as those of Apollo at Delphi or Artemis at Ephesus, were often granted the right of asylum (ἀσυλία) by kings: people who fled there could not be seized. Demetrius offers Jerusalem the same status. Israel's law knew a narrower asylum at the altar for those who had killed by accident (Exodus 21:13–14; 1 Kings 1:50–53), and the cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–15).

a: they did not trust them or accept them
p: Jonathan refused the richer offer: he remembered Demetrius's past and judged the future.
b: The writer gives one reason: they remembered the harm Demetrius had done (Bacchides, Alcimus, Nicanor). Historians add that Jonathan may have judged Alexander, backed by Rome, Pergamum and Egypt, likely to win. He also already held from Alexander what mattered most, the high priesthood. Josephus, retelling the chapter, passes over the people's answer in silence and goes straight to the battle (Antiquities 13.58–61).

t: The death of Demetrius I, 150 BC
p: Demetrius died fighting; Josephus says his horse stuck in a swamp and he was surrounded.
b: Josephus adds that Demetrius fought bravely, but his horse became stuck in a marsh, and he was killed by arrows (Antiquities 13.59–61). Polybius, who knew Demetrius in Rome and helped him escape, wrote warmly of him in his earlier years (Polybius 31.11–15). His sons fled; one of them returned in 147 BC as Demetrius II (10:67).

p: Ptolemy's daughter married three Seleucid kings in turn and later ruled in her own name.
b: Cleopatra Thea was the daughter of Ptolemy VI and Cleopatra II. She married Alexander Balas in 150 BC (10:58), was taken from him and given to Demetrius II (11:12), and later married his brother Antiochus VII. She ruled for a time in her own right and is shown on coins. She is a distant relative of the famous Cleopatra VII, Antony's queen, a century later. The "year 162" is 150 BC.

p: The marriage alliance between Egypt and Syria recalls Daniel's "daughter of the king of the south".
b: Daniel 11 describes the long wars between "the king of the north" (the Seleucids) and "the king of the south" (the Ptolemies), and two marriage alliances that failed (Daniel 11:6; Daniel 11:17). Cleopatra's two marriages fit the same pattern, though they come after the events Daniel describes. 1 Maccabees tells the story without comment, but by 11:12 this alliance too has broken.

p: The Greek calls Jonathan's accusers "pestilent men": a Hebrew way of saying they were a menace.
b: ἄνδρες λοιμοί, literally "pestilence men", is the Greek of the Old Testament for "worthless men" or troublemakers: the Greek of 1 Samuel 2:12 renders the Hebrew "sons of worthlessness" for Eli's sons as υἱοὶ λοιμοί, "sons of pestilence", and Acts 24:5 calls Paul "a plague". The accusers came from Jonathan's own people, the Hellenizing party. The king's refusal to hear them shows the change of power.

p: A Jew is dressed in royal clothes by a foreign king, while his enemies are put to shame.
b: The scene follows a known pattern: Pharaoh dressed Joseph in fine linen and gave him a gold chain (Genesis 41:42), and the Persian king had Mordecai led through the city in royal robes while Haman proclaimed his honor (Esther 6:7–11; Esther 8:15). Here too the herald goes through the city (10:63), and Jonathan's accusers flee (10:64). Early readers would have heard the echo.

p: Jonathan becomes the king's own general and governor of Judea, a Seleucid office as well as a Jewish one.
b: στρατηγός is "general" or "governor", and μεριδάρχης is the governor of a district (meris). With these titles Jonathan is no longer only the leader of a Jewish party; he is the royal official for his region. The KJV, following the Latin, renders μεριδάρχης as "partaker of his dominion" (see the variant).

a: Demetrius son of Demetrius came from Crete
p: The son of Demetrius I lands with Cretan mercenaries to win back his father's throne.
b: The young Demetrius II, later called Nicator, had been kept safe at Cnidus. In the year 165 (147 BC) he landed with mercenaries from Crete, led by Lasthenes (11:31–32). Josephus adds that he sailed to Cilicia with mercenaries provided by Lasthenes the Cretan (Antiquities 13.86). His campaign set off the battles of 10:69–89 and the fall of Alexander in chapter 11.

p: "Hollow Syria": the Seleucid name for southern Syria and Palestine.
b: Κοίλη Συρία, "Hollow Syria", first meant the Beqaa valley between the Lebanon ranges, and then the whole southern part of the kingdom, including Judea and the coast. It was the land the Ptolemies and Seleucids fought over for a century (Daniel 11). Apollonius, its governor, should have been Alexander's man; he declared for Demetrius, and Jamnia on the coast became his base.

a: Why do you lord it over us in the mountains?
p: Apollonius taunts Jonathan for fighting only in the hills, where cavalry are useless.
b: The challenge rests on real military facts: the Jewish army fought best in hills and passes, while the Seleucids' strength was cavalry and the phalanx on open ground. Apollonius dares Jonathan to come down to the coastal plain. The Arameans of 1 Kings 20:23 reason the same way: "Their god is a god of the mountains." Jonathan accepts and wins on the plain (10:77–85).

a: your fathers were routed twice in their own land
p: Which two defeats? Perhaps the loss of the ark and Saul's death, both at Philistine hands.
b: Apollonius does not say which defeats he means, and scholars have guessed. Many think of the Philistine victories at Aphek, where the ark was taken (1 Samuel 4), and at Gilboa, where Saul and Jonathan died (1 Samuel 31). Both were won by the people of the coastal plain, the very ground Apollonius now holds. Others think of more recent defeats, such as Judas's death (9:18). The taunt fits a governor who speaks for the coastal cities (10:71).

p: Jaffa, Judea's natural port; holding it gave the Jews access to the sea.
b: Joppa (Jaffa, now part of Tel Aviv) was the port for Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 2:16; Jonah 1:3). Judas had once punished its people for drowning Jews (2 Maccabees 12:3–7). Jonathan takes it here, and Simon later settles Jews there and calls it Judea's gateway to the sea (14:5). Acts tells of Peter at Joppa (Acts 9:36–43; Acts 10:5).

a: Beth-dagon, the temple of their idol
t: The temple of Dagon at Ashdod
p: Dagon's temple at Ashdod, where the ark once humbled Dagon's statue, is burned by Jonathan.
b: Azotus is Ashdod, one of the five Philistine cities. There the Philistines once placed the captured ark beside Dagon, and the statue fell face down before it (1 Samuel 5:2–5). The temple still stood in Jonathan's time, under the old name Beth-dagon, "house of Dagon". The writer lets the echo stand: the God who toppled Dagon's statue now lets his people burn Dagon's house. The book does not say whether the place was spared from the law's command to destroy idol shrines (Deuteronomy 7:5); Jonathan simply burns it.

a: and those who had fled into it
t: Burning the temple with people inside
p: Jonathan burns the temple with refugees inside; the book records it without regret.
b: Eight thousand dead, many of them burned in a temple where they had fled for safety (10:85), is a hard scene. The writer counts it as a victory over idolatry and over the cities of the coast that had threatened Judea (5:68). Some modern readers see here the darker side of the Hasmonean wars, which later included the forced conversion of the Idumeans (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258). For the question whether Christians may fight in war, see the card at Deuteronomy 20.

t: The gold brooch of the Kinsmen
p: A gold clasp for the purple cloak was the mark of the highest court rank, the King's Kinsmen.
b: The πόρπη was the clasp that held a cloak at the shoulder. A gold one was the sign of the "Kinsmen" (συγγενεῖς), the top rank at court. Jonathan now outranks the First Friends of 10:65. The young Antiochus VI will confirm the same privilege (11:58). Simon later uses it as a mark of rule that no one else in Judea may wear (14:43–44).

t: Ekron, a Philistine city given to Jonathan
p: The first city outside Judea to become a Hasmonean possession, by royal gift.
b: Ekron, one of the five Philistine cities (Joshua 13:3; 1 Samuel 5:10), lay on the plain west of Judea. Alexander gave it to Jonathan as a κληροδοσία, a grant of land held as an inheritance. It is the first piece of foreign territory the Hasmoneans held, and a sign of their move from defending the Torah to building a state.

a: as many as the sand on the seashore
t: Like the sand of the sea
p: An old biblical picture for a huge army, used of Israel's enemies in Joshua and Judges.
b: The kings of Canaan came out against Joshua "as many as the sand on the seashore" (Joshua 11:4), and the Midianites' camels were like the sand (Judges 7:12). The same picture is used in 1 Samuel 13:5 for the Philistines at Michmash. The writer gives Ptolemy VI the size of Israel's old enemies, though here he is the threat to Alexander, not to Jonathan.

t: Did Ptolemy plot from the start?
p: 1 Maccabees says Ptolemy came to steal the kingdom; other ancient writers tell it in Ptolemy's favor.
b: 1 Maccabees says Ptolemy VI came "by trickery" to seize Alexander's kingdom. Josephus, retelling it, says rather that Ptolemy came to help his son-in-law and turned against him only after an attempt on his life by Alexander's minister Ammonius (Antiquities 13.103–110). Diodorus and Polybius describe Ptolemy as a mild and honest king. Some historians prefer Josephus's account here, and some suggest that 1 Maccabees reflects Judean hostility toward a king who had backed Onias IV's rival temple in Egypt.

a: the temple of Dagon burned down
p: Azotus's people show the king the ruins Jonathan left, hoping he will punish Jonathan; he stays silent.
b: The scene is a petition from the coastal cities: the burned temple of 10:84, the torn-down suburbs, and heaps of corpses left on the road. The king's silence (11:5) is a political choice: Jonathan was the ally of his son-in-law, and Ptolemy needed him quiet while he took the coast. The heaps (θιμωνιαί) are the word used for sheaves stacked on a threshing floor.

p: The Nahr el-Kebir, on today's border of Lebanon and Syria: the old northern limit of Ptolemaic claims.
b: The Eleutherus ("Free River") runs into the sea north of Tripoli. It had long been treated as the border between Seleucid Syria and the southern lands that the Ptolemies had once ruled. Jonathan escorting Ptolemy that far shows how high he stood: a Jewish high priest seeing a king to the edge of his old domain. Jonathan comes back to it in 12:30.

a: He put two crowns on his head
p: Ptolemy put on the crowns of Asia and Egypt; Josephus agrees, but says he soon gave Syria up to Demetrius.
b: 1 Maccabees says Ptolemy VI wore both crowns, ruling Egypt and the Seleucid lands at once. Josephus also says the people of Antioch and the army made him king, so that he put on two diadems, the one of Asia and the other of Egypt; but he adds that Ptolemy soon persuaded them to accept Demetrius II, saying he was content with Egypt, to avoid the envy of the Romans (Antiquities 13.113–115). Diodorus says he declined the Syrian diadem (32.9c). The accounts differ less on the crowns than on how long Ptolemy kept them. The "crown" here is a διάδημα, a white band tied round the head, the mark of a Hellenistic king.
orig: περιέθετο δύο διαδήματα περὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ

a: Zabdiel the Arab cut off Alexander's head
t: The end of Alexander Balas, 145 BC
p: Alexander fled to an Arab chief who killed him and sent his head to Ptolemy.
b: Alexander lost the battle near the Oenoparas River in Syria (Strabo 16.2.8) and fled to the Arabs, where Zabdiel, a local chief, beheaded him. Josephus gives the same story and the same name (Antiquities 13.118). Sending the head was proof of death. Ptolemy, wounded in the battle, saw it before he died (11:18).

a: King Ptolemy died on the third day
p: Ptolemy died of wounds from the battle; his Egyptian garrisons in Syria were wiped out.
b: Ptolemy VI Philometor fell from his horse in the battle and died some days later, in 145 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.117–119). His death ended Egypt's attempt to win back the coast. The garrisons he had left in every town (11:3) were killed, and Demetrius II took the throne without the Egyptian army that had put him there. The "year 167" is 145 BC.

a: some men who hated their own nation
p: Jews who opposed the Hasmoneans: in the book's eyes, traitors; to some historians, the losers of a civil war.
b: The writer gives Jonathan's Jewish opponents no voice: they "hate their nation" and are "lawless" (11:25). Many historians read the conflict as a civil war among Jews, between the Hasmonean party and others, including priestly families who had held power before and Jews who welcomed Greek ways. The book records the Hasmonean side. The Citadel's garrison included both foreign soldiers and such Jews (6:21; 10:14).
orig: μισοῦντες τὸ ἔθνος αὐτῶν, ἄνδρες παράνομοι

a: he gave orders to keep up the siege
p: Jonathan leaves the siege running and goes in person to a king who is angry with him.
b: Jonathan neither obeyed nor openly defied the king. He kept up the siege, took a delegation of elders and priests, and went with gifts. Hellenistic kings sometimes arrested or killed client rulers who came to them, as Tryphon later did to Jonathan himself at Ptolemais (12:48). "He put himself in danger" says the writer knew the risk.

p: A large sum, perhaps about 9 tonnes of silver, offered to buy freedom from tribute.
b: A talent of silver weighed about 26–34 kg (57–75 pounds), so three hundred talents was some 8–10 tonnes. Jonathan offers a single payment in place of yearly tribute. The indemnity Rome imposed on Antiochus III in 188 BC was 15,000 talents in all, 12,000 of them paid over twelve years, and Jason had offered 360 talents and more for the high priesthood (2 Maccabees 4:8–9). Whether Jonathan paid is not said.

p: A court title for the king's chief minister, as Joseph was "a father to Pharaoh".
b: Lasthenes, who brought the Cretan mercenaries (10:67), was the young king's chief minister. "Father" was an honorary title for the highest official of a Hellenistic court; Joseph says God made him "a father to Pharaoh" (Genesis 45:8), and Haman is called the king's "second father" in the Greek additions to Esther. In 11:31 he is also "our Kinsman".

p: The districts promised in 10:30 are now named: Ephraim, Lod and Ramathaim.
b: Aphairema is probably Ephraim or Ophrah, northeast of Bethel (John 11:54). Lydda is Lod, on the road from Joppa (Acts 9:32). Rathamin is Ramathaim, often taken as the home of Samuel and of Joseph of Arimathea. Their transfer from Samaria to Judea brought Jewish villages under Jerusalem's rule and widened Judea to the northwest.

a: for all who sacrifice in Jerusalem
p: A definition of the Jews by their worship, which leaves out the Samaritans of Gerizim.
b: The phrase marks out who benefits: those who bring sacrifices to Jerusalem, as against those who worship on Mount Gerizim. It is the language of a royal official describing a temple community. The Samaritans had their own temple, which was laid waste when John Hyrcanus took Shechem and Gerizim late in the century (Josephus, Antiquities 13.255–256).

a: put up on the holy mountain
p: Royal grants were set up in public, often cut in stone in a temple.
b: Hellenistic kings had grants to cities and temples inscribed on stone and set up in temples, where they served as proof of rights. Many such inscriptions survive. Simon later had the people's decree in his honor written on bronze tablets and set up on Mount Zion (14:26–27, 48). None of the Jerusalem copies survive.

a: All the troops who had served his fathers came to hate him
t: Demetrius II sends his army home
p: Demetrius dismissed the regular army and kept his foreign mercenaries; the veterans turned against him.
b: To save money, Demetrius II disbanded the old royal troops and relied on the mercenaries from Crete and the islands. Ancient writers agree that this cost him the kingdom: Diodorus (33.4) and Josephus (Antiquities 13.129–130) both blame the cruelty of his mercenaries and the anger of the dismissed troops. Tryphon used the discontent at once (11:39).

p: Diodotus Tryphon, a former officer of Alexander's, who used the boy Antiochus and later took the throne himself.
b: Tryphon, whose own name was Diodotus, had served Alexander Balas. He fetched Alexander's son from an Arab chief and crowned him as Antiochus VI (11:54). He later had Jonathan seized and killed (12:39–48; 13:23), murdered the boy king and ruled in his own name (13:31–32). Coins of both survive. Diodorus calls him Diodotus Tryphon (33.4a).

p: An Arab chief who was raising the young son of Alexander; Josephus calls him Malchus.
b: The name, spelled several ways in the manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Venetus have Imalkue), probably reflects the Semitic name Malik, "king". Josephus calls him Malchus (Antiquities 13.131), and Diodorus calls the guardian Iamblichus (33.4a). The boy had been sent to him for safety while his father lost the war.

a: I will greatly honor you and your nation
p: Demetrius promises more than he gives; the writer prepares the reader for 11:53.
b: "I will glorify you with glory" is a royal promise, and the writer quotes it in full so that the betrayal in 11:53 will be felt. The book's view of foreign kings is consistent: their promises shift with their needs. Psalm 146:3 gives the older wisdom: "Do not rely on nobles."

a: about a hundred and twenty thousand men
p: Antioch's people rose against Demetrius II; Jewish troops crushed the revolt and saved him.
b: Antioch was one of the largest cities in the world, but the numbers (120,000 rioters, 100,000 dead) are the round, swollen figures of ancient war stories. Josephus and Diodorus also tell of a revolt in Antioch against Demetrius II, put down with great bloodshed by his mercenaries (Josephus, Antiquities 13.133–142; Diodorus 33.4). Only 1 Maccabees and Josephus give the Jewish troops the leading role. The episode shows how far the Hasmonean army had come: from a band in the hills to the force that saved a king in his own capital.

a: That day they killed about a hundred thousand in the city
t: Jewish soldiers in a Gentile city
p: The writer celebrates the Jewish troops; modern readers note the slaughter of a city's people.
b: The writer counts the day as glory for the Jews (11:51) and makes no moral comment on the killing and burning of the city. Readers have noted the irony that the Hasmoneans, who rose against a Seleucid king's violence, here kill the Seleucid capital's people for another Seleucid king. Josephus describes the fire spreading through the whole city (Antiquities 13.139). For the debate on violence in these books, see the Deuteronomy 20 card.

a: Give us your right hand in peace
p: To give the right hand was to give a sworn promise of safety: the normal sign of surrender on terms.
b: δεξιὰς δοῦναι, "to give right hands", meant a promise of safe conduct or peace terms (6:58; 11:62, 66; 13:45). The hand was a pledge, as in Galatians 2:9, where the apostles give Paul "the right hand of fellowship". The people of Antioch ask the king for terms so that the Jews will stop.

a: But he proved false in everything he had said
p: Demetrius breaks his word; Josephus says he even demanded the old tribute back.
b: Josephus, retelling it, says Demetrius demanded all the tributes the Jews had paid to the earlier kings (Antiquities 13.143). For the writer this is the pattern of every king except Rome's Senate (chapter 8). Jonathan's change of sides to Antiochus VI (11:57) is justified by it.

p: War elephants were the royal army's heavy force; taking them meant taking the kingdom's power.
b: The Seleucids kept a herd of war elephants at Apamea, though the treaty with Rome after 188 BC had forbidden them (1:17; 6:30–37; 8:6). Taking the elephants and Antioch was the decisive step for Tryphon. Coins of Antiochus VI show an elephant.

p: Judea's three new districts plus a fourth, perhaps Akrabattene or Perea.
b: Demetrius had given three districts (11:34). Antiochus VI now speaks of four. The fourth is not named. Many think it was Akrabattene, southeast of Shechem (5:3), or a district east of the Jordan. The grant shows the young king outbidding Demetrius, as Demetrius once outbid Alexander.

p: Royal privileges marked a ruler as the king's own Kinsman: gold dishes, purple and the gold brooch.
b: The right to drink from gold and to wear purple was a privilege the king granted to his highest men. Gold cups in a king's hall appear also in Esther 1:7 and Daniel 5:2–3. Jonathan already had the brooch from Alexander (10:89); Antiochus confirms it. The list returns in the people's decree for Simon (14:43–44).

p: The steep headland south of Tyre, where the coast road climbs over the cliffs: the border of Phoenicia.
b: The "Ladder of Tyre" is the coastal ridge at Ras en-Naqura (Rosh HaNiqra), on today's border of Israel and Lebanon, where the road was cut in steps. Josephus places it about 100 stades (about 18 km) north of Ptolemais (Jewish War 2.188). Simon's command from there to Egypt's border covered the whole coast of Palestine: a royal office, not a Jewish one.

p: Probably the old Persian name for the lands west of the Euphrates, here the Syrian province; some take it as the land beyond the Jordan.
b: πέραν τοῦ ποταμοῦ, "beyond the river", was the Persian name for the province west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10–11; Ezra 8:36), and 7:8 uses it so for the province Bacchides governed. Here it most likely has the same sense: Jonathan, newly made the young king's ally, travels through the province of Syria, whose troops rally to him, and then turns south to Ascalon and Gaza. Some readers take "the river" as the Jordan and the phrase as the land across it. The Plain writes "beyond the River" in lower case because the Greek has no word for "province" here.

a: He took the sons of their rulers as hostages
p: Jonathan now does what Bacchides had done to Judea (9:53): hold the sons of leaders.
b: The reversal is neat. In 9:53 Bacchides took the sons of Judea's leaders as hostages to the Citadel; now Jonathan takes the sons of Gaza's leaders to Jerusalem. The Hasmoneans are behaving as a regional power. Gaza remained a free city until Alexander Jannaeus destroyed it, about 96 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.358–364).

p: Kedesh of Naphtali, an old city of refuge in upper Galilee, then held by Tyre.
b: Kedesh (Tel Qedesh), northwest of Lake Huleh, was a city of refuge in the land of Naphtali (Joshua 20:7) and the home of Barak (Judges 4:6). In the Hellenistic period it lay in the territory of Tyre; excavators have found a large Persian and Hellenistic administrative building there, with about 2,000 clay seal impressions, abandoned in about the 140s BC. Demetrius's officers came there to stop Jonathan from taking Galilee.

p: The Sea of Galilee: Gennesar is the name Luke uses for the lake.
b: Gennesar or Gennesaret is the plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, and its name was given to the lake itself: "the lake of Gennesaret" (Luke 5:1). The Old Testament calls it Kinnereth (Numbers 34:11). Jonathan camped by the lake and marched north at dawn to the plain of Hazor, about 15 km (9 miles) away.

p: The great Canaanite city where Joshua beat the kings of the north: the same plain, the same kind of foe.
b: Alexandrinus reads "Nasor", but Sinaiticus has Hazor, and Josephus places the battle in "the plain of Hazor" (Antiquities 13.158); see the variant. Hazor "had been the head of all these kingdoms" when Joshua fought Jabin and his allies there (Joshua 11:10; see Joshua 11:1–11). Judges 4 tells of a later Jabin of Hazor beaten by Barak of Kedesh, the very town of 11:63. The writer's readers would hear the echo: Jonathan fights the "foreigners" on the old battlefield of the conquest.

a: Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Chalphi
p: Two officers stayed when the army fled; Absalom's family appears again in 13:11.
b: A Jonathan son of Absalom leads Simon's troops to Joppa in 13:11, so this Mattathias may be his brother. Chalphi is the Greek form of a Semitic name like Halphai (compare "James son of Alphaeus", Matthew 10:3). The two who stand are a small echo of the brave few in the stories of the judges and of David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:9–12).

a: Jonathan tore his clothes, put dirt on his head and prayed
p: Joshua did the same after the defeat at Ai, before the Lord turned the battle.
b: After Israel fled before Ai, Joshua tore his clothes, fell before the ark, and the elders "threw dust on their heads" (Joshua 7:6). The same signs of grief mark Mattathias (2:14), Judas at Mizpah (3:47) and the people at the ruined Temple (4:39). Here they lead straight to victory. The writer does not give the prayer's words: as often in this book, God is not named, but the turn of the battle follows prayer.
orig: καὶ ἐπέθετο γῆν ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ, καὶ προσηύξατο

a: About three thousand of the foreigners fell that day
p: The win at Hazor kept Galilee open to Jonathan; it ends the chapter on a note of strength.
b: The "foreigners" (ἀλλόφυλοι) are the troops of Demetrius II, whom the writer calls by the old word for Philistines. The victory let Jonathan keep his gains under Antiochus VI and turn to Rome and Sparta in chapter 12. The next time he trusts a Seleucid general, Tryphon, it will cost him his life (12:48).
